title: Building nuclear’s next-gen workforce
summary: As the nuclear energy industry advances a new generation of more cost-effective, more efficient small reactors, another challenge is coming into sharper focus: Who will build, operate, and maintain them? The Department of Energy projects that the nuclear energy sector will need more than 375,000 skilled workers by 2050 to sustain existing nuclear power operations and support deployment of next-gen reactors. Meeting that demand will require a workforce pipeline that begins well before someone walks through the doors of a nuclear facility for the first time. The Nuclear Energy Academic Roadmap (NEAR) was created to address the critical need for a skilled nuclear energy workforce.

title: Pacific Fusion receives N.M. radioactive materials license
summary: The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) has approved Pacific Fusion’s radioactive materials license, allowing it to fabricate and test deuterium-tritium fusion targets and conduct experiments at a facility that is under construction in Albuquerque, N.M., the company announced. The license authorizes up to 15,000 curies (around 1.5 grams) of tritium, although the company said it “never intends to have an inventory that exceeds 10,000 curies.” The license also authorizes the use of materials needed to store tritium and support diagnostics and fusion operations.

title: Comments close soon on PRM for fuel reprocessing plants
summary: Members of the public have until 11:59 p.m. (EST) on Monday, November 23, to submit comments to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regarding a petition for rulemaking (PRM) that proposes changes to the way irradiated fuel reprocessing plants are regulated. If the updates that the petition suggests are accepted, fuel reprocessing facilities that handle quantities of strategic special nuclear material (SSNM) large enough to support commercial production would be required to follow the same material control and accounting (MC&A) requirements as other nuclear fuel facilities not covered by an exception. The effect would be a tightening of the regulations that govern reprocessing plants, compared with those currently in effect.

title: Bechtel Says Poland Agreement ‘Opens New Chapter’ In Nuclear Cooperation
summary: Bechtel, Gdańsk University of Technology and the University of South Carolina, have signed a memorandum of cooperation that “opens a new chapter” in nuclear energy cooperation between the academic communities of Poland and the US. Bechtel, a key partner in the construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant, which will be built at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in the Pomerania region in the north of the country, said the agreement builds on its existing partnership with the University of South Carolina’s Molinaroli College of Engineering and Computing, announced in October 2026, which established a fund to support nuclear education and workforce development.

title: Norway Consortium Gets €1.8 Million Towards Development Of Nuclear Power For Maritime Industry
summary: Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder Vard and offshore service vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK20m (€1.8m, $2m) in government funding to develop an integrated nuclear power system for the maritime industry. The marine nuclear propulsion system (MarNuPS) project, led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, aims to move the technology from engineering studies into full-scale testing, with a first vessel deployment targeted for 2031 or 2032.
